title: Confidence Intervals for a Proportion
trouble: Students say there is a 95% chance the true value is in this particular interval.

blocks.html: A poll finds that 60% of 150 adults read a book last month. The true proportion of all adults is unknown, and a different sample would give a different $\hat{p}$. The sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$ tells us how far $\hat{p}$ typically lands from $p$, and the inverse normal tells us how many standard deviations cover the middle 95%. Together they give an interval of plausible values.

A confidence interval for a proportion is $$\hat{p} \pm z^*\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}},$$ estimate ± margin of error. The critical value $z^*$ sets the confidence level: $1.645$ for 90%, $1.960$ for 95%, $2.576$ for 99%. Use it when the sample is random and there are at least 10 successes and 10 failures.

About 95% of all samples give a $\hat{p}$ within $1.96\sigma_{\hat{p}}$ of the true $p$. Distance is symmetric: if $\hat{p}$ is within $1.96\sigma_{\hat{p}}$ of $p$, then $p$ is within $1.96\sigma_{\hat{p}}$ of $\hat{p}$. So the interval $\hat{p} \pm 1.96\sigma_{\hat{p}}$ captures $p$ for about 95% of samples. We do not know $p$, so we estimate $\sigma_{\hat{p}}$ with the standard error $\sqrt{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})/n}$. The $1.96$ is the z with 97.5% of the area to its left, leaving 2.5% in each tail.

opts.task: Take 100 samples at 95%. About how many intervals miss the true p? Then switch to 80% and 99% and compare the widths.

blocks.cap: Each line is the interval from one random sample. The true p never moves; the intervals do.

blocks.title: Building the interval
blocks.q: In a random sample of 150 adults, 90 read a book last month. Find a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all adults who did.
steps: $\hat{p} = \dfrac{90}{150} = 0.6$. Conditions: random sample; 90 successes and 60 failures, both at least 10.
We are 95% confident that between about 52% and 68% of all adults read a book last month.

blocks.title: Higher confidence
blocks.q: Find a 99% interval from the same sample.
steps: More confidence costs a wider interval.

blocks.title: What "95% confident" means
blocks.q: A student says: "There is a 95% probability that the true proportion is between 0.522 and 0.678." What is wrong?
steps: The true proportion is a fixed number. This interval either contains it or it does not; there is nothing random left.
The 95% describes the method: if we took many samples and built an interval from each, about 95% of those intervals would capture $p$.
blocks.a: The 95% is a property of the method, not of one interval.

blocks.html: Saying there is a 95% chance that the true value is in this particular interval. Check your sentence: put the confidence on the method ("95% of intervals built this way capture $p$") or use the phrase "we are 95% confident that…" for this interval.

The interval only accounts for random sampling error. A biased sample can miss the truth by far more than any margin of error. The econometrics course has a machine that builds 100 intervals at a time.
